content.p: On the afternoon of Sunday 30 January 1972, soldiers of the Parachute Regiment drove into the Bogside district of Derry and opened fire on people who had been taking part in, or had been near, a civil rights march. Thirteen people died that day. A fourteenth man, John Johnston, who had been wounded earlier in the afternoon, died on 16 June 1972. No soldier was injured, and, according to a chronology compiled at Ulster University, no guns or bombs were recovered at the scene of the shootings.

The army's account, accepted in large part by the first official inquiry later in 1972, was that its men had come under attack from gunmen and bombers. A second inquiry, which took 12 years, rejected that account in June 2010 and the Prime Minister apologised in Parliament. Only one former soldier was ever put on trial. On 23 October 2025 a judge at Belfast Crown Court found him not guilty on every count, while saying that the paratroopers on duty that day had lost all military discipline.

The march had its roots in the introduction of internment on 9 August 1971, when 342 people were arrested in raids across Northern Ireland and held without trial. The CAIN chronology records an immediate surge in violence, with 17 people killed over the next 48 hours, ten of them Catholic civilians shot by the British Army. Internment ran until December 1975, and of the 1,981 people detained in that time, 1,874 were Catholic or republican and 107 Protestant or loyalist.

On 18 January 1972 Northern Ireland's prime minister, Brian Faulkner, banned all parades and marches until the end of the year. Four days later an anti-internment march at Magilligan strand, in County Derry, was stopped by soldiers from the Green Jackets and the Parachute Regiment. The army fired rubber bullets and CS gas at close range. Some witnesses claimed that paratroopers bused in from Belfast beat protesters and had to be held back by their own officers.

The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association planned another anti-internment march in Derry for 30 January. On 24 January the senior RUC officer in the city, Chief Superintendent Frank Lagan, told the army brigade commander, Andrew MacLellan, that the demonstration would be non-violent and asked that it not be met with military intervention. MacLellan agreed to recommend that to General Robert Ford, then Commander of Land Forces. But Ford had already put Lieutenant Colonel Derek Wilford, who commanded the 1st Battalion of the Parachute Regiment, in charge of an arrest operation, and on 25 January he put MacLellan in overall command of the operation to contain the march. The chronology adds that Edward Heath, the prime minister, confirmed on 19 April 1972 that the plan to arrest rioters had been known to government ministers beforehand.

Two days before the march, on 27 January, two RUC officers, Peter Gilgun and David Montgomery, were shot dead in an attack on their patrol car on the Creggan Road. According to a Channel 4 documentary of 1992 cited in the chronology, the Stormont MP Ivan Cooper, who helped organise the march, had obtained assurances that the IRA would keep out of the area during it.

The march was due to leave the Creggan estate at 2 p.m. and reach the Guildhall for a rally. It set off about 2.50 p.m., and people joined along the route. Estimates of its size differ: some observers said as many as 20,000, while the Widgery report put it at between 3,000 and 5,000. Al Jazeera, writing in 2025, said more than 10,000 marched.

Army barriers blocked the way into the city centre. Around 3.45 p.m. most marchers followed the organisers' instructions and turned toward Free Derry Corner for a meeting. A section of the crowd went on to the barrier in William Street, where a riot developed. The chronology notes that many observers described the rioting as not especially intense.

At about 3.55 p.m., out of sight of the meeting, soldiers in a derelict building in William Street fired five rounds and wounded Damien Donaghy, 15, and John Johnston, 59. The chronology says more recent research suggests an Official IRA member then fired a single shot back. Around the same time paratroopers asked permission to begin their arrest operation. At about 4.07 p.m. Support Company of the 1st Battalion was ordered into William Street. The order said the soldiers were "not to conduct running battle down Rossville Street". Saville later found that Wilford either deliberately disobeyed that limit or failed for no good reason to understand it, and that he did not pass the brigadier's instruction to Major Ted Loden, who commanded Support Company.

The soldiers did chase people down Rossville Street. Saville wrote, as the Guardian quoted him, that the chase swept up both rioters and many peaceful marchers, leaving soldiers no means of telling them apart. At about 4.10 p.m. Support Company began firing in the area of the Rossville Flats, and by about 4.40 p.m. it was over. The chronology places the shooting in four areas: the car park and the forecourt of the flats, the barricade on Rossville Street, and the area around Glenfada Park. British Army evidence, as it summarises, was that 21 soldiers fired 108 rounds.

The families who spoke in 2010 and 2025 gave the dead faces and ages. Jackie Duddy's brother Joe said Jackie was running away from the soldiers when he was shot. Tony Doherty, whose father Paddy died, told the crowd outside the Guildhall that the dead and wounded were civil rights marchers who were innocent, one and all. Michael McKinney's brother William was 27 and was shot in the back, he said, while running away from the protest. The Public Prosecution Service gives William McKinney's age as 26, while CBC and Al Jazeera's 2003 report give 27.

Jim Wray, 22, was shot in the back and, his brother Liam said in 2010, shot again as he lay dying. According to the chronology, forensic evidence put to the Saville inquiry in September 1999 indicated that Wray was hit in the back while already down. Counts of the wounded vary by source: the chronology says 14 were wounded by gunfire and one of them later died, while NPR and CBC say 15 were wounded.
content.h2: The first account and the Widgery report
content.p: The next day the Home Secretary, Reginald Maudling, told the Commons that the army had returned fire with aimed shots, injuring people who were attacking with firearms and bombs. On 1 February Heath named Lord Widgery, the Lord Chief Justice, to inquire. In Derry the choice was met with scepticism and some groups at first called for non-participation, the chronology says. Eleven of the dead were buried in the Creggan on 2 February. In Dublin the day was marked by a work stoppage and a march of about 100,000 people, and the British Embassy was burned to the ground.

Widgery heard 114 witnesses in 17 sessions at Coleraine between 21 February and 14 March 1972, with three further sessions in London, and delivered his report on 10 April. It was published on 18 April. NPR describes a 39-page report produced in barely two months. It said the soldiers' firing "bordered on the reckless", but accepted their claim that they were responding to IRA attacks and Widgery said he suspected that some of the dead "had been firing weapons or handling bombs in the course of the afternoon". In Derry it was nicknamed the "Widgery Whitewash". In a December 1992 letter to John Hume, John Major wrote that the government had said in 1974 that the dead were to be seen as innocent of any allegation of handling firearms or explosives.

Evidence given to the later inquiry cast doubt on how the army's version took shape. Al Jazeera reported in 2003 that disclosed documents suggested the "terrorists on the demo" narrative came from Captain Michael Jackson, then adjutant of the battalion, and that a list of 15 supposed "engagements" attributed to Major Loden did not match where the dead were found. Michael Mansfield QC, for some of the families, called the list an attempt to fabricate evidence. A handwritten manuscript in Jackson's hand that tallied with the list then emerged from the Ministry of Defence, and Loden called it mysterious and nothing to do with him.

Tony Blair announced a new inquiry on 29 January 1998, and it opened at the Guildhall in Derry on 3 April 1998 under Lord Saville, with the retired New Zealand judge Edward Somers and William Hoyt, a judge from Canada. Somers stood down in 2000 and John Toohey replaced him. Soldiers were offered immunity from prosecution for their evidence, and the inquiry gave them partial anonymity. In 1999 the High Court and Court of Appeal allowed 17 paratroopers to stay anonymous, and in November 2001 36 soldiers won a High Court ruling letting them give evidence by video link, and in 2002 the inquiry moved temporarily to Britain to hear the paratroopers who fired. Martin McGuinness confirmed on 3 May 2001 that he had been the IRA's second-in-command in Derry at the time. The main hearings closed in November 2004.

The report was published on 15 June 2010. NPR described the inquiry as the longest in British history, with more than 900 witnesses over 400 days and a cost of about $300 million. Its main findings, as the Guardian set them out:

None of the casualties shot by Support Company was armed with a firearm, and "with the probable exception of Gerald Donaghey" none had a bomb. None posed a threat of causing death or serious injury, and no warning was given before the soldiers fired. Saville rejected the soldiers' claims that they had fired in response to nail or petrol bombers, concluding that no one threw or threatened to throw such a bomb. He found that many soldiers had "knowingly put forward false accounts in order to seek to justify their firing". The troops had been driven by a mistaken belief that republican paramilitaries were responding in force, based on shots first fired by one soldier, Lieutenant N, and there had been "a serious and widespread loss of fire discipline".

The report did not find a plan to shoot selected ringleaders, nor that the state had authorised unwarranted lethal force. It found that Ford "neither knew nor had reason to know" that his decision to deploy the paratroopers would lead to unjustified firing. It said republican paramilitaries had fired some shots, and that two Official IRA men had gone to a sniping position, but none of that justified the shooting of the civilians. McGuinness was "probably armed with a Thompson sub-machine gun", it said, but there was no evidence he fired it. Saville called Bloody Sunday a catastrophe for the people of Northern Ireland that strengthened the Provisional IRA and increased nationalist hostility toward the army.

Cameron told the Commons that what happened was "both unjustified and unjustifiable" and "wrong", and apologised on behalf of the state. A crowd outside the Guildhall in Derry cheered as the families, who had read the findings inside, gave a thumbs-up from the windows. Stephen Pollard, a solicitor for soldiers who gave evidence, said the evidence had been "cherry-picked" and that he would fight any prosecution. Saville had said that the soldiers' own inquiry evidence could not be used against them in later criminal proceedings.

After the report, the director of public prosecutions in Northern Ireland said he was considering whether murder, perjury or perverting the course of justice charges could arise. The Public Prosecution Service announced its decisions on 14 March 2019: Soldier F would be prosecuted, and other soldiers who fired shots would not. Al Jazeera reported that 16 other former soldiers were ruled out for insufficient evidence. In July 2021 the service decided not to proceed against Soldier F, after a May 2021 court ruling that evidence relied on against two other former soldiers, Soldiers A and C, was inadmissible. A judicial review led to a Divisional Court ruling on 23 March 2022, and on 22 September 2022 the service said it would recommence proceedings.

Soldier F, a former lance corporal, denied all seven charges. Two were murder, for the deaths of Jim Wray and William McKinney. Five were attempted murder, with four named wounded men (Friel, Quinn, Mahon and O'Donnell) and further people not identified in the charge. The judge-only trial lasted about a month. Soldier F sat behind a curtain, did not testify and called no evidence; in a 2016 police interview he had said he had no reliable recollection of the day. The prosecution rested on statements that Soldiers G and H gave to the Royal Military Police in 1972. G is dead and H refused to testify, so neither could be cross-examined.

The verdict came on 23 October 2025: Judge Patrick Lynch acquitted Soldier F of all seven counts. The Crown's evidence fell "well short" of proof beyond reasonable doubt, he said, and delay had seriously hampered the defence in testing the hearsay statements. He said there was no concept of "collective guilt" and that the prosecution had not shown Soldier F was knowingly and intentionally assisting in the shootings or was shooting himself with intent to kill. He also said the paratroopers had "totally lost all sense of military discipline" and that those responsible "should hang their heads in shame".

The Public Prosecution Service said there is no mechanism to appeal an acquittal after a Crown Court trial. Mickey McKinney said Soldier F's discharge from the dock was "one million miles" from an honourable discharge and blamed the British state, the RUC and the army. Michelle O'Neill, Northern Ireland's First Minister, called the verdict deeply disappointing. Northern Ireland's veterans commissioner, David Johnstone, hoped the ruling would end a long process for the soldier. The families' solicitor Ciaran Shiels said they were awaiting a prosecution service review of alleged perjury.
